title: Taswira · From Kanem to Bornu

clips.disputed: The Bulala are said to have taken Njimi in 1363 by one account, or to have driven the Sayfawa out by 1376 and taken Kanem by 1388 by another. The move to Bornu is dated about 1380 or about 1387, and Ngazargamu's founding from about 1460 to about 1488.

features.name: Lake Chad
features.location: The dot marks today's lake, and the background draws today's outline. That is not the shoreline of any period in this chapter; no older shoreline is drawn, because none has been sourced.

features.name: Kanem
features.location: A regional anchor at today's Mao, not a capital. Njimi is not placed, and Tié's exact position has not been checked for this page. The ring marks the region.
features.disputed: Kanem's founding is usually dated to about 700, but some sources give about 600 or about 900.

features.name: Bulala (Lake Fitri)
features.location: Drawn at Lake Fitri. Where the Bulala rulers sat while they held Kanem is not placed.

features.name: Bornu, west of the lake
features.location: A regional anchor at the site of the later capital, Ngazargamu, inside a wide ring. Where the court stayed between the 1380s and Ngazargamu's founding is not placed.

features.name: The Kanembu move west to Bornu
features.location: Schematic: from the Kanem region to the land west of the lake. The way they went, and where the court stopped before Ngazargamu, are not drawn.

lc-chad-kanem.title: Chad: a country study, "Precolonial history: Kanem-Borno"
lc-chad-kanem.author: Federal Research Division, Library of Congress (ed. Thomas Collelo)
lc-chad-kanem.kind: government reference work (secondary); seen only in search excerpts
lc-chad-kanem.rights: US government work; facts cited, no text reused.
lc-chad-kanem.checked: Not opened: this session's network policy blocked the site, so the page was seen only through web-search excerpts on 31 Oct 2026. The nomadic Sayfawa pushed south into Kanem before the twelfth century; Bulala invaders from around Lake Fitri, to the east, killed five of the six mais who reigned between 1376 and 1400; they forced Mai Umar Idrismi to leave Njimi and move the Kanembu to Borno; the Kanuri emerged from intermarriage of Kanembu and Borno peoples; Kanem-Borno peaked under Mai Idris Aluma (about 1571-1603), who required major political figures to live at court and made alliances by marriage; by the early nineteenth century the empire was in decline, and in 1808 Fulani warriors conquered Ngazargamu.

By 1376 the Bulala (Bilala) had driven the Sayfawa from their capital and by 1388 had taken Kanem; another account dates the capture of Njimi to 1363. They ruled Kanem until they lost it about 1630 (in the 17th century), after which they settled around Lake Fitri.

Core territory in Kanem, north-east of Lake Chad; the site of Njimi has never been located; founding typically dated to c. 700, with c. 600 and c. 900 also given; the Bilala took Njimi around 1380 and the court moved to Bornu; exported salt, ivory, slaves and animal products.

Built by Mai Ali Gaji (Ali Gazi), in the fork of the Komadugu Gana and Komadugu Yobe near today's Geidam, Yobe State; the first lasting capital after the loss of Njimi; abandoned in the early 1800s in the Fulani war. Its founding is dated about 1460, about 1462, by 1472 and about 1488 in different copies and articles, and Ali Gaji's reign 1455-1487, 1470-1503 or 1472-1504.

Lake Mega-Chad's highstand lasted until about 5,000 years ago, then levels fell rapidly across the basin; the northern basin (the Bodele depression, today the world's greatest dust source) held a small lake until about 1,000 years ago, when it became dry.
